## Self-Guided Approximation of Markov Decision Processes {#s01 .cover .speaker-change data-background-color="#30353b"}

::: {.slide-body}
<div class="cover-subtitle">A Guided Tour</div>
:::

::: {.notes}
This talk retains the tutorial introduction and focuses on self-guided ALPs for continuous state and action MDPs. Numerical results use the final Pakiman, Nadarajah, Soheili, and Lin (2025) paper. The discrete tutorial is covered in a cited handoff. Bermudan options are in technical backup. Main-talk interactions require no Python.
:::

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
Source: [Tutorial §4, inventory example](assets/tutorial.pdf). Illustrative two-day path. Start with the inventory scale, ordering, and the demand distribution. The first click shows costs and the inventory update. The second starts the two-day simulation. Follow the inventory marker through each event.

Allow about two minutes for audience participation. Ask for a show of hands: order 2, 4, or 6 units?
Invite one brief explanation, set the chosen quantity, and place the order. Pause at the prediction
prompt before revealing demand. After the first outcome, ask how the carried stock or backlog should
affect the next order. Participants with laptops can make their own choices; everyone can participate
in the projected example. The three suggested quantities keep the room discussion focused; the slider allows integer order quantities from 0 to 6.

If time permits, replay the same demands with another first order and compare costs. Explain that
this comparison uses known outcomes and does not establish which policy has the lowest expected cost.
Close by asking what information the next decision needs: the stock or backlog carried forward.
This example introduces sequential decisions and feedback. Adapting a decision to a state is distinct
from the adaptation of an approximation that the tutorial develops later.

Begin with zero units in stock. Choose each order before revealing its demand. Each day independently draws an integer from 1 through 5, each with probability 1/5. This teaching distribution differs from the truncated-normal distribution used later in the full inventory model. Default orders are 2 and 1. One possible demand path, 5 then 3, gives 3 units of unmet demand and then
5, as in the static fallback. Ordering 6 units initially instead gives 1 unit left over after demand 5. Other
runs can have different outcomes. A stockout here means demand that cannot be filled immediately; it waits as
backlog and is filled by a later order. Show how carried stock or backlog changes the supply available from
the second order. Purchases cost $20 per unit, holding costs $1 per unit per day, and backlogged demand
costs
$25 per unit per day. Displayed costs are realized and undiscounted, not the infinite-horizon objective or expected costs. This introductory model carries all unmet demand forward at the displayed $25/unit/day rate;
it does not apply backlog limits or lost-sales penalties. The later inventory model introduces the
manuscript's bounds and additional costs. New run clears the old demands; Replay same demands retains the
completed path so participants can compare different order choices fairly. The latter is a counterfactual
replay of known outcomes, not a new unpredictable run. Neither order is claimed optimal.
:::

<div class="mdp-objective fragment" data-fragment-index="4">
 <div>
  <strong>Policy optimization</strong>
  <div class="mdp-formula"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mtext>\min_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t c(s_t,\pi_t(s_t))\,\middle|\,s_0\right]</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t c(s_t,\pi_t(s_t))\,\middle|\,s_0\right]</annotation></semantics></math></div>

<!-- FOOTER: shared author names and university logos. -->
{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
The current state and action determine the next-state distribution. An action is one order, and a policy specifies the order to place at each observed state. Reveal the transition, the expected period cost, and then the policy optimization problem. The opening simulation illustrates two decisions. For this objective, continue the inventory system over an infinite horizon and discount period t by gamma to the power t, with 0 < gamma < 1. The cost c averages the period expense over demand conditional on the state and action. The outer expectation averages the trajectory induced by the policy, given the initial inventory. The state includes backlog, and all unmet demand carries forward in this introductory model. The cost function is stationary. The table permits time-dependent policies and transitions; the later discounted-MDP formulation also uses stationary dynamics.
:::

## Why Solving the MDP Becomes Difficult {#s07 .content-slide .bellman-growth}

<!-- SLIDE CONTENT -->

::: {.slide-body}
::: {.growth-bellman-equation}
<h3>Bellman optimality equation</h3>

$$
\underbrace{V^*(s)}_{\text{optimal value function}}=\min_{a\in\mathcal A(s)}\left\{\underbrace{c(s,a)}_{\text{immediate cost}}+\underbrace{\gamma\int_{\mathcal S}V^*(s')\,P(ds'\mid s,a)}_{\text{discounted expected future cost}}\right\},\qquad s\in\mathcal S.
$$
:::


<!-- FOOTER: shared author names and university logos. -->
{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
Source: [Tutorial introduction and §2.1](assets/tutorial.pdf) · Bellman equation in costs; illustrative counts

The equation is stationary and discounted. At a fixed state, compare feasible actions using cost now plus discounted expected future cost. The optimal value function is V*, with no time index.

First advance reveals the product-count card. Say that a tabular calculation must
represent values for states and compare feasible actions. The number of candidate joint actions shown is
before shared constraints are applied. The counter is a separate scaling illustration with 15 inventory
levels and four order choices per product; it does not enumerate reachable states in the two period demo,
whose order choices were 0 to 6.

Start with one product and ask how adding a second product changes the two counts. Pause for answers before moving the slider to two
products. States increase from 15 to 225, while candidate actions increase from 4 to 16. Each additional
product multiplies the counts by 15 and 4, respectively. Then move the slider further to show how quickly
this growth compounds. Reset returns the counter to one product. After reaching 30 products, the next three clicks reveal continuity, lead times, and perishability. The continuous
case motivates approximations that exploit structure, and it does not claim that all exact methods
enumerate every state and action.

These are Cartesian-product counts, not counts of all reachable states in the manuscript instance. The slider
ranges from 1 to 30 products, with 15 inventory levels and 4 order choices per product. Counts are calculated
exactly; displays from one billion onward use approximate scientific notation, with the full integer available
on hover. Shared constraints can eliminate action combinations but leave a difficult combinatorial search. The
toy counter never enumerates the state space. The continuous case refers to states and actions ranging over
nontrivial intervals.
:::

```{=html}

 <div class="bridge-formulation bridge-policy">
  <h3>Policy optimization</h3>
  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mtext>\min_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t c(s_t,\pi(s_t))\,\middle|\,s_0=s\right].</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t c(s_t,\pi(s_t))\,\middle|\,s_0=s\right].</annotation></semantics></math>
 </div>
 <div class="bridge-formulation bridge-bellman fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
  <h3>Stochastic dynamic program <span style="color:#6f7f8a;font-size:.8em;font-weight:400">(Bellman optimality equation)</span></h3>
  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mtext>V^*(s)=\min_{a\in\mathcal A(s)}\left\{\underbrace{c(s,a)}_{\text{immediate cost}}+\underbrace{\gamma\int_{\mathcal S}V^*(s&#39;)\,P(ds&#39;\mid s,a)}_{\text{discounted expected future cost}}\right\},\qquad s\in\mathcal S.</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^*(s)=\min_{a\in\mathcal A(s)}\left\{\underbrace{c(s,a)}_{\text{immediate cost}}+\underbrace{\gamma\int_{\mathcal S}V^*(s&#39;)\,P(ds&#39;\mid s,a)}_{\text{discounted expected future cost}}\right\},\qquad s\in\mathcal S.</annotation></semantics></math>
 </div>
<div class="bridge-lp-reveal fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
 <div class="bridge-formulation bridge-lp">
  <h3>Exact linear program</h3>
  <div class="bridge-lp-row bridge-elp-stack">

\displaystyle\max_{V:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R}\quad\phantom{\int_{\mathcal S}\!} &amp; \phantom{V(s)\,\nu(ds)}\\[8pt]
\text{s.t.} &amp; V(s)\le c(s,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal S}V(s&#39;)\,P(ds&#39;\mid s,a),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal S,\ a\in\mathcal A(s).
\end{array}</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{array}{l@{}l}

\text{s.t.} &amp; V(s)\le c(s,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal S}V(s&#39;)\,P(ds&#39;\mid s,a),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal S,\ a\in\mathcal A(s).
\end{array}</annotation></semantics></math>

    </svg>
   </div>

\displaystyle\max_{V:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R}\quad\int_{\mathcal S}\! &amp; V(s)\,\nu(ds)\\[8pt]
\text{s.t.} &amp; V(s)\le c(s,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal S}V(s&#39;)\,P(ds&#39;\mid s,a),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal S,\ a\in\mathcal A(s).
\end{array}</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{array}{l@{}l}
\displaystyle\max_{V:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R}\quad\int_{\mathcal S}\! &amp; V(s)\,\nu(ds)\\[8pt]
\text{s.t.} &amp; V(s)\le c(s,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal S}V(s&#39;)\,P(ds&#39;\mid s,a),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal S,\ a\in\mathcal A(s).
\end{array}</annotation></semantics></math>
   </div>

<aside class="notes"><p>Source: tutorial §4.1 and self-guided ALP paper §2. Recall the infinite-horizon discounted policy objective on page 4. Time-homogeneous costs and transitions, 0 &lt; gamma &lt; 1, and standard discounted-MDP boundedness/integrability and regularity assumptions are understood. An optimal stationary policy exists under the assumptions used here. Initially show only policy optimization. First click reveals the stochastic dynamic program. Second click reveals the variable domain and Bellman inequalities, with a red arrow replacing equality by less than or equal to. The third click reveals the state-relevance-weighted objective. The hidden objective keeps its space, preserving the alignment of V across the two LP rows. At V star the Bellman minimum implies an inequality for every feasible action. For a candidate V impose all such inequalities simultaneously: V ≤ TV. Monotonicity and discounted contraction imply that a feasible V lies below V star; V star is feasible and pointwise maximal. Maximizing the state-relevance-weighted integral recovers the largest feasible lower bound. Replacing the Bellman equation by inequalities alone is not sufficient; maximization is essential. Nu is a state relevance distribution, not necessarily the initial state distribution. Pointwise recovery from this particular weighted objective needs appropriate support and regularity. The following slide illustrates the maximization with a schematic feasible family, not a numerical solver.</p></aside>
```

```{=html}
<aside class="notes"><p>The curves are schematic. The target is piecewise linear, with a steeper shortage side and kinks at two inventory levels. They are not outputs from the numerical inventory model. The displayed family consists of constant downward shifts V_delta = V star minus delta, with delta at least zero. In a discounted cost MDP, the Bellman operator obeys T(V star minus delta) = V star minus gamma delta. Thus every such shift satisfies the Bellman inequalities. Maximization raises the moving feasible function and its state-relevance-weighted objective toward V star. The shaded gap shrinks as it rises. Faint curves remain as reference feasible functions. After the animation finishes, the next click rewrites the objective as an expectation under nu, the state relevance distribution. The marked states then receive illustrative masses 10%, 15%, 40%, 25%, and 10%. These normalized discrete weights illustrate nu, and do not alter the simulated family of value functions. Early Next clicks are ignored until animation completion. Use Replay animation to repeat.</p></aside>
```

## Approximate Linear Program {#s27 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide}

::: {.slide-body}

<div class="badge">Theory · §4.1</div>

<h3>ALP Construction</h3>

<div class="alp-inputs">
<div class="equation-box alp-input">
<p><strong>Features or basis functions</strong></p>

$\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_N:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb R$

<p>Choose the functions used to represent value.</p>
</div>
<div class="equation-box alp-input">
<p><strong>Weights</strong></p>

$\beta:=(\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_N)\in\mathbb R^{N+1}$

<p>Optimize the coefficients of the approximation.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="equation-box compact-equation fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<p class="center"><strong>Finite-dimensional value function approximation (VFA)</strong></p>

$$
V_\beta(s)=\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_n\varphi_n(s),
\qquad \beta\in\mathbb R^{N+1}
$$
</div>

<div class="equation-box compact-equation fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left:3px solid var(--accent)">
<p class="center"><strong>Semi-infinite approximate linear program (ALP)</strong></p>

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\beta\in\mathbb R^{N+1}}\quad
    & \mathbb E_\nu[V_\beta(s)] \\
\text{s.t.}\quad
    & V_\beta(s) \le c(s,a)
      +\gamma\,\mathbb E[V_\beta(S')\mid s,a], \quad \forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}(s).
\end{aligned}
$$


</div>

:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Introduce the two top boxes: fixed features or basis functions on the left and optimized weights on the right. Advance to combine them into the finite-dimensional VFA, then advance to the semi-infinite ALP below it. The coefficient vector is finite, but feasibility must hold for every continuous state and every feasible action in the set A. That is the tension driving Section 4: the representation is compact, while finding the important constraints remains difficult.
:::

```{=html}
<span class="cmp-step-trigger fragment" data-cmp-step="2" data-fragment-index="1" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="cmp-step-trigger fragment" data-cmp-step="3" data-fragment-index="2" aria-hidden="true"></span>
</div><div class="cmp-discussion-stage fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><div class="cmp-discussion"><p>Please see the discussions in de Farias and Van Roy (2003) and Proposition 4 of the paper for why both the choice of <strong>features</strong> and the <strong>state-relevance weights</strong> directly affect policy quality.</p></div><div class="alp-inputs cmp-choice-definitions"><div class="equation-box alp-input"><p><strong>Features</strong></p><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mtext>\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_N</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_N</annotation></semantics></math></div><div class="equation-box alp-input"><p><strong>State relevance distribution</strong></p><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mtext>\nu:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R</annotation></semantics></math></div></div></div></div>
<aside class="notes"><p>On entry, compare the labeled regression observations with the shaded ALP-feasible region below its boundary. The shading denotes candidate value functions V feasible to ALP; the boundary curve is unchanged. First advance shows a comparison table with feature, approximation, and optimization rows and fits an affine model on both sides. Second advance expands each feature set to include the squared input. Point out the remaining regression residuals and the gaps between the ALP curve and its ceiling. The table keeps the ML and ALP choices parallel after the first click. Both models begin with uniform weights. Third advance reveals the weights row and changes the importance of observations through wᵢ and the importance of states through ν. The feature sets stay quadratic for both refits. In cost minimization, full Bellman feasibility implies Vβ ≤ V*, so minimizing the ν-weighted absolute error is equivalent to maximizing the ν-weighted value. Optimal value labels are unnecessary for the ALP solve. The next slide asks how to refine these feature and relevance choices.</p><p>The nine ML inputs are equally spaced from 0 to 1; the responses in that order are 1.05, .77, .99, .58, .77, .89, .52, 1.00, 1.48. Absolute-deviation regression gives the affine fit .74 + .24x. Adding x² yields 1.05 − 1.55x + 1.98x². The unweighted sum of absolute errors falls from 1.790 to 1.214375; six observations still have nonzero residuals. On the final advance, assign weights 4, 4, 4 to the three rightmost observations and weight 1 to each remaining observation. The weighted refit is approximately 1.173333 − 3.731429x + 4.038095x². Under the new weights the total weighted absolute error falls from 3.287188 for the old curve to 2.287619 for the refit.</p><p>The ALP illustration is a one-action discounted self-loop on [0,1], with c(s)=(1−γ)(.6+.9s³). Each Bellman inequality reduces to Vβ(s)≤f(s)=.6+.9s³. Initially ν is continuous Uniform[0,1], so its density is one and the objective is the unweighted integral against ds. The optimal affine lower bound is the tangent to f at the uniform mean .5, namely .375+.675s, with uniform objective .7125. Adding s² gives the optimal quadratic .6−.4s+1.2s², with uniform objective .8. Its Bellman gap is .9s(s−2/3)². The probability measure with mass 1/4 at zero and 3/4 at 2/3 has the same first two moments as Uniform[0,1]; evaluating the binding constraints at those nodes proves optimality among feasible quadratics. The final weights replace the uniform distribution by atomic masses (.25,.05,.70) at states (0,.3,.9). The resulting m=Eν[S²]/Eν[S] is about .886, giving q(s)=.6+.9(2ms²−m²s). Its new weighted objective is 1.055738, compared with 1.0278 for the previous quadratic under those same updated weights. Bellman constraints and features are unchanged by the weight update. Circle area represents probability.</p></aside>
```

::: {.notes}
Source: Tutorial §4.3. Introduce two approximation choices: the basis family representing the value function and the state relevance distribution nu defining the ALP objective. First reveal random features as a way to enrich the representation. Then reveal self guidance as a way to adapt effective state relevance through guiding constraints. The density sketches are conceptual illustrations of weighting states. The quadratic is an example of an initial representation; it has not been optimized in an earlier continuous method in this main talk. Fixed basis functions do not mean fixed coefficients.
:::

## Random Features {#s38 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide .random-feature-slide}

::: {.slide-body}


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<div class="equation-box compact-equation">
<p class="center"><strong>Example: quadratic VFA</strong></p>

$$
V_{\beta}(s)=\beta_0+\beta_1s+\beta_2s^2.
$$
</div>
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<div class="equation-box compact-equation fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<p class="center"><strong>Random feature representation</strong></p>

$$
\begin{gathered}
\theta_n\overset{iid}{\sim}\vartheta,\\
\varphi_n(s)=\phi\!\left(\theta_{n0}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\theta_{ni}s_i\right),\\
V_N(s;\beta)=\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\varphi_n(s).
\end{gathered}
$$
</div>
:::
:::

<div class="feature-family-formulas fragment" data-fragment-index="1">

 <div class="feature-relu"><strong>ReLU</strong> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mtext>\varphi_\theta(s)=\max\{0,b+ws\};\quad\theta=(b,w)</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varphi_\theta(s)=\max\{0,b+ws\};\quad\theta=(b,w)</annotation></semantics></math></div>

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
This slide contrasts a fixed quadratic approximation with nested random features. Fourier is on the left in blue and ReLU is on the right in purple. After the formulas, reveal one sampled pair and its feature curve in each panel. The next two clicks replace both samples and curves. The samples are illustrative. The later ReLU fits use unit slopes and sampled hinge locations. Use seed 17 and a fixed pool of 48 features, displaying only 1, 3, 5, 12, and 24 features. Each plot refits least-squares coefficients to the same illustrative target, so grid RMSE decreases along the sequence. The target illustrates approximation capacity and is not the optimal inventory value function. The two families use the same state grid, target function, vertical scale, and quadratic reference.
:::

## Feature-Based ALP (FALP): Theoretical Guarantees {#s39 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide}

::: {.slide-body}
<div class="falp-stages">
<div class="falp-construction-grid fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1">
<div class="step-card">
<p class="derivation-label"><span class="step-number">1</span>Generate the VFA</p>
<p>Draw $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_N\sim\vartheta$ and fix the random features $\varphi_n$.</p>

$$
V_N(s;\beta)=\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\varphi_n(s).
$$
</div>
<div class="step-card falp-model-card fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<p class="derivation-label"><span class="step-number">2</span>Solve FALP</p>

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\beta\in\mathbb R^{N+1}}\quad
&\mathbb E_{\nu}[V_N(s;\beta)]\\
\text{s.t.}\quad
&V_N(s;\beta)
\le c(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb E[V_N(S^{\prime};\beta)\mid s,a], \\ &\forall s\in\mathcal{S},\ a\in\mathcal{A}(s).
\end{aligned}
$$
</div>
</div>
<div class="theorem-box falp-convergence fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
<h3 class="falp-theorem-title">Theorem 1</h3>
<p class="falp-theorem-setup">Under Assumptions 1–3, let $\beta_N^{\mathrm{FA}}$ be any finite optimal FALP solution and write $V_N(s):=V_N(s;\beta_N^{\mathrm{FA}})$.</p>
<div class="falp-theorem-part">
<h4><span>(a)</span> Valid lower bound</h4>

$$
V_N(s)\le V^*(s),\quad \forall s\in\mathcal S
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbb E_{\nu}[V_N]\le\mathbb E_{\nu}[V^*].
$$

</div>
<div class="falp-theorem-part fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
<h4><span>(b)</span> High-probability VFA guarantee</h4>
<p>Suppose the feature-sampling density satisfies $\rho(\theta)\ge\underline\rho>0$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$. For any $\delta\in(0,1]$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the sampled features,</p>

$$
0\le\lVert V^*-V_N\rVert_{1,\nu}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\right).
$$

</div>
</div>
</div>
:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Source: Pakiman et al., Self-Guided Approximate Linear Programs, Management Science 71(4), 2025, Theorem 1, p. 3389 (local assets/self-guided-alp.pdf). The first click reveals Solve FALP; the next replaces both construction steps with this theorem in the title-page dark palette. V_N abbreviates the random-feature approximation at a finite optimal FALP solution. Part (a) is pointwise Bellman feasibility and its state-relevance-weighted lower-bound consequence. Part (b) holds with probability at least 1-delta over the independently sampled feature parameters, not in expectation. The paper uses delta in (0,1]. Assumptions 1–3 provide MDP regularity and compactness, representability of V* by the universal Lipschitz feature family, bounded features with finite sampling second moment, and existence of a finite FALP optimum. In the integral representation, $V^*(s)=\beta_0^*+\int_\Theta B^*(\theta)\varphi(s;\theta)\,d\theta$; $\lVert B^*/\rho\rVert_{2,\rho}$ is the rho-weighted L2 norm of B*/rho. The density rho corresponds to the feature-sampling distribution vartheta in Step 1. D_s is the state-space radius, not its dimension. The guarantee controls weighted L1 value-function error; it does not guarantee monotonically improving greedy-policy cost.
:::

## Functional Central Limit Theorem {#feature-monte-carlo .content-slide .fclt-slide background-color="#30353b"}

::: {.slide-body}
<div class="functional-clt" data-functional-clt>
<svg class="fclt-chart" viewBox="0 0 1120 350" role="img" aria-labelledby="fclt-chart-title fclt-chart-desc"><title id="fclt-chart-title">Function estimates concentrate around the unknown optimal value function</title><desc id="fclt-chart-desc">Repeated averages of independent random functions cluster around a reference curve. A linked normal distribution at a selected state narrows at the inverse square root rate. Click the function plot to inspect another state.</desc></svg>
<div class="fclt-legend"><span class="fclt-key-target">$V^*$ · unknown reference</span><span class="fclt-key-estimates">Averages $\widehat V_N$</span><span class="fclt-key-new">New function contributions</span></div>
<div class="fclt-toolbar"><div class="fclt-counts" aria-label="Feature count"><span data-fclt-stage="1">1</span><span data-fclt-stage="4">4</span><span data-fclt-stage="16">16</span><span data-fclt-stage="64">64</span><span data-fclt-stage="256">256</span></div><span class="fclt-spread">Spread: <strong data-fclt-spread>1.00</strong> × initial</span><div class="fclt-buttons"><button type="button" data-fclt-play>Animate</button><button type="button" data-fclt-replay>New draws</button></div></div>
<div class="fclt-conclusion fragment" data-fragment-index="4">

$$
\bigl\lVert V^*-\widehat V_N\bigr\rVert_{1,\nu}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\right)\ \longrightarrow\ 0.
$$

</div>
<span class="fclt-trigger fragment" data-fragment-index="0" data-fclt-n="4" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="fclt-trigger fragment" data-fragment-index="1" data-fclt-n="16" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="fclt-trigger fragment" data-fragment-index="2" data-fclt-n="64" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="fclt-trigger fragment" data-fragment-index="3" data-fclt-n="256" aria-hidden="true"></span>
</div>
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a Gaussian-limit illustration of functional central-limit behavior, not an additional theorem about the optimized FALP solution. The orange curve represents the unknown optimal value function solely as a schematic reference. The simulation uses independent smooth random-function contributions F_i(s)=V*(s)+sum_k Z_ik psi_k(s), where the Z_ik are independent standard normal coefficients and the six smooth basis functions are fixed. Each displayed estimate averages N such contributions; the different teal curves are independent repetitions with nested draws. Thus the means have pointwise variance sigma(s)^2/N and are exactly Gaussian in this illustrative model for every N. At a selected state, the right plot is that exact normal marginal, centered at V*(s0); its density axis rescales and is labeled with its current peak. For more general function-valued summands, a functional CLT requires appropriate moment and tightness conditions: the centered, sqrt(N)-scaled average can converge in distribution to a Gaussian process. The unscaled estimates concentrate at their mean, not at a nondegenerate normal distribution. Actual FALP coefficients are optimized under Bellman constraints and are not sample-mean coefficients; Theorem 1 on the previous page establishes a high-probability approximation bound, not a Gaussian limit. This simulation does not use V* as available training data or claim that the illustration solves an MDP. Advance through N=1,4,16,64,256, then reveal the functional CLT. Animate runs the same sequence automatically; New draws starts independent repetitions. Selecting a different state updates both the probe and the normal marginal.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the opening question before showing the warehouses. Reveal the true costs, then the first estimates and the choice of North. Add features, show the improved estimates, and reveal the switch to South. V-star(North)=9 and V-star(South)=10 are audience references, unknown to the policy. Before, V_N=(3,4); after, V_(N+B)=(9,8). Both approximations are no greater than truth and improve pointwise. The policy compares approximate continuation costs with equal immediate costs, so it first selects North and then South. The selected continuation cost increases from 9 to 10. These values illustrate a possible local ranking reversal; they are not outputs of an asserted particular random-feature draw or a full FALP solve. A discounted absorbing-future model with gamma=0.9 and per-period costs 0.9 and 1 realizes the displayed true future values. Both approximations satisfy the absorbing-state Bellman inequalities. Add a decision state with zero-cost transitions to the futures and set its approximation to gamma times the smaller approximate future value to extend feasibility. Thus better approximation, even pointwise, does not alone imply a monotonically better greedy policy. Do not interpret the example as denying convergence under additional assumptions. A final click replaces the illustration with the norm comparison: decreasing weighted L1 approximation error from N to N+B does not imply decreasing PC_chi of the greedy policy. PC_chi denotes discounted policy cost from initial-state distribution chi. The statement concerns the absence of a monotonicity guarantee; it does not assert that every feature addition worsens policy performance.
:::

FALP retains Bellman inequalities only; self-guided FALP also keeps its own previous solution as a statewise floor. The plots share a fixed vertical scale and the same illustrative optimal value function. Orange bands on the FALP state axis identify where the current approximation dips below its previous value. Curves illustrate the distinction rather than report numerical LP solves: FALP may cross its predecessor, whereas the self-guided VFA stays above its previous guide. This does not imply monotonically improving greedy-policy costs.

Settings: MDP seed 12345, feature seed 111, 3,000 sampled Bellman constraints, 3,000 guide states, 1,000 demand samples, and one new Fourier feature per stage. The first two plots show the logarithm of positive value-function approximations on identical fixed vertical scales. State relevance starts uniform on [-4,12]. The third panel uses the actual nonnegative HiGHS shadow prices of each stage's guiding constraints. The effective finite-sample measure is (nu + sum_j lambda_j delta_sj)/(1+sum_j lambda_j). The displayed curve smooths only the atomic component with boundary-normalized Gaussian kernels of bandwidth .65; this does not change the solver. There is no update when all guide multipliers are zero, even if some guide constraints happen to be tight. Amber marks on the guided VFA and under the density identify exactly the same states with positive guide shadow prices. The density panel is synchronized with the two VFA panels on each click. At N=3, the next click shows the reweighting formula and identifies the dual variable. The base objective distribution stays uniform. The effective relevance is its dual interpretation. The estimates are precomputed; no audience-side Python is required.
:::

## Self-Guided ALP: Theoretical Results {#sg-theory .content-slide .continuous-import-slide .speaker-change .sg-theory-slide data-background-color="#30353b"}

::: {.slide-body}
<div class="sg-inventory-theory">
<h3>Proposition 5</h3>
<p class="sg-theory-setup">For self-guided FALP with exact constraints, let $V_N^{\mathrm{SG}}$ denote a finite optimal VFA with $N=qB$ features, $q\ge1$.</p>

$$
V_0^{\mathrm{FA}}(s)=V_0^{\mathrm{SG}}(s)
\le V_B^{\mathrm{SG}}(s)\le\cdots\le V_N^{\mathrm{SG}}(s)\le V^*(s),
\qquad \forall s\in\mathcal S.
$$

<p class="sg-theory-norm-label">Hence, for <u>every</u> fixed state-relevance distribution $\nu$,</p>

$$
\bigl\lVert V^*-V_N^{\mathrm{SG}}\bigr\rVert_{1,\nu}
\le
\bigl\lVert V^*-V_{N-B}^{\mathrm{SG}}\bigr\rVert_{1,\nu}.
$$

<p class="sg-theory-policy fragment" data-fragment-index="0">The <strong>worst-case greedy-policy performance bound</strong> in Proposition 4 also improves.</p>
</div>
:::

::: {.notes}
Proposition 5 (Pakiman et al., 2025, printed p. 3393) gives a pointwise nondecreasing sequence of finite-optimal self-guided VFAs bounded above by the optimal value. Integrating the pointwise error gives the inequality for every fixed state-relevance distribution. On the next click, cite Proposition 4 (printed p. 3391) for the worst-case greedy-policy performance bound discussed after Proposition 5. The theorem uses exact Bellman and guiding constraints. The inventory example on the preceding slide illustrates the mechanism with sampled constraints.
:::

<div class="inv-expanded-dimension fragment" data-fragment-index="1">State dimension: $L+(J-1)=5+(6-1)=\mathbf{10}$.</div>
<div class="inv-expanded-cost fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
<h3>Expected one-period cost</h3>
<div class="inv-cost-decomposition"><div class="inv-cost-order"><strong>Ordering</strong><small>Paid on receipt</small></div><div class="inv-cost-hold"><strong>Holding</strong><small>Stock carried over</small></div><div class="inv-cost-backlog"><strong>Backlog</strong><small>Unfilled demand</small></div><div class="inv-cost-lost"><strong>Lost sales</strong><small>Beyond backlog limit</small></div><div class="inv-cost-expired"><strong>Disposal</strong><small>Expired units</small></div></div>

```{=html}
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c(s,a)={}\textcolor{#285b78}{\gamma^J c_o a}\ +\ \mathbb E_D\Bigg[ \textcolor{#1c6558}{c_h\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}s_i-(D-s_0)^+\Big)^+} +\textcolor{#9b622d}{c_b\Big(D-\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}s_i\Big)^+} +\textcolor{#963f3d}{c_l\Big(\underline s+D-\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}s_i\Big)^+} +\textcolor{#78508d}{c_d(s_0-D)^+}\Bigg].</annotation></semantics></math>
```

</div>
</div>
</div>
:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Source: Pakiman et al. (2025), Self-Guided Approximate Linear Programs, §6.1, pp. 3397–3398 (assets/self-guided-alp.pdf). Start with only the scalar inventory-level graphic from page 15. First click replaces it with the five expiry coordinates for lifetime L=5. The next adds five pipeline coordinates for lead time J=6 and the ten-dimensional-state count L+(J−1). The final click adds the familiar five-part expected cost decomposition. There is no action, demand-distribution, or transition section. Capital L replaces the paper's lifetime symbol throughout this slide. At the decision epoch, s0 expires this period and si has i periods until expiry; uj arrives in j periods. For nonnegative age coordinates these describe physical stock. In backlogged states s0 may be negative and the coordinates are notional, with signed sum representing total inventory/backlog. The cost matches the paper: ordering is paid on receipt, giving gamma^J c_o a in this equivalent formulation. Holding is assessed on stock after demand and expiration, backlog is unmet demand, and lost sales exceed the backlog capacity. The symbol underline s is the negative backlog bound. Disposal is c_d(s0−D)^+ for expired units. It is not salvage revenue and is not an additional sixth cost category. The scalar model on page 15 disposes of capacity overflow; here the paper's disposal term concerns expired stock. Generic cost coefficients distinguish this paper instance from page 15's illustrative numeric costs. Expectations are over demand D; this retains the cost's economic decomposition without repeating the full transition equations.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three future-work ideas from the user-provided AC_ALP_Rewritten synopsis. These are illustrative research sketches, not reported inventory results or additional guarantees from the published paper. Click through the three pictures or use Play all. First, adapt feature sampling using current-policy visits, restrictive Bellman constraints, and successor observations. The first picture shifts a normalized schematic sampling density and draws new purple feature centers from feedback-directed regions. Second, add one randomly selected feature at a time. Select its center and bandwidth before the convex subproblem; they are not additional optimization variables. Retain the entire existing VFA as a fixed aggregate and optimize only its common rescaling alpha and the new feature's coefficient beta. Previously fitted coefficients are not independently refitted. The middle picture repeats fix aggregate → add one feature → fix the resulting aggregate. Its curves use three illustrative two-variable convex least-squares fits solely to animate this representation; the unseen demonstration target is not an available optimal MDP value function, and this picture is not an AC-ALP solve. Third, learn which state-action regions are most restrictive and concentrate search and transition observations where uncertainty could change that assessment. The final picture shows qualitative learned importance and shrinking uncertainty, with no empirical policy-cost or convergence claims.
:::
